# The ISLA forward pass {#sec-architecture}

**This chapter states exactly what ISLA computes, stage by stage, with one
name for every quantity and the tensor shape beside it.** @sec-isla explains
why each part is there; this chapter is the reference for *what* the class
does, and it is the one description of the architecture that the other
chapters and the code are held to. Read it with @fig-isla-pass open: every
stage below is one box of that figure, and every equation names the
identifier that computes it in `physicsnemo/experimental/models/isla/model.py`.
The structure is written for a width $d$, a stack of 12 slice layers and
$M = 256$ slices, the class's layer and slice counts; nothing in it depends
on those numbers, and the width the recipe runs is stated with the commands
in @sec-using-config.

```{python}
#| label: setup-arch
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
from matplotlib.colors import Normalize
```

## Notation {#sec-arch-notation}

**One symbol per quantity, one code name per symbol.** Indices: $i, j$ run
over the $N$ tokens, $s, t$ over the $M$ slices, $k$ over the $K$ global
vector inputs. Batch axes are omitted throughout; the code carries a
leading batch dimension on every tensor.

| symbol | shape | code | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| $x_i, n_i, w_i$ | $N{\times}3,\ N{\times}3,\ N$ | `points`, `normals`, `measure_weights` | sampled boundary positions, outward normals, the surface area each sample stands for |
| $g_k$, $\sigma$ | $K{\times}3$, $S$ | `global_inputs` (rank 1, rank 0) | the problem's global directions and scalars, as named fields (external aerodynamics, the benchmark instance: $K = 1$, the far-field flow direction; $S = 0$ on the surface tasks, $S = 1$ on AirfRANS) |\n| $v_{ip}$, $T_{iq}$ | $N{\times}P{\times}3$, $N{\times}Q{\times}3{\times}3$ | `boundary_inputs`, `query_inputs` (rank 1, rank 2) | per-token tensor inputs (a prescribed traction, a prescribed stress); $P = Q = 0$ on the aerodynamic tasks |
| $\hat g_k$, $\hat n_i$ | $K{\times}3$, $N{\times}3$ | `g_unit`, `n_hat` | the same directions and normals, normalized to unit length |
| $L$ | scalar | `gauge` | the length unit: the measure-weighted RMS pairwise distance of the sample |
| $r_i$ | $N{\times}3$ | `r` | position in length units, $x_i / L$; used only inside differences |
| $\ell_i$ | $N$ | `log_w` | $\log w_i$, the measure bias of every routing softmax |
| $s_i$ | $N{\times}(K + n_b + S)$ | `invariants` | the seed: the scalars a token knows before any layer runs ($n_b$ counts the boundary inputs' invariants) |
| $h_i$ | $N{\times}d$ | `h` | the token state, width $d$ (`hidden`) |
| $\lambda_{is}$, $\lambda'_{is}$ | $N{\times}M$ | `logits`, `logits + bias` | routing logits before and after the geometric refinement |
| $a_{is}$ | $N{\times}M$ | `a` | routing weights: a softmax over tokens $i$ for each slice $s$ |
| $z_s, m_s$ | $M{\times}3$ | `z_pos`, `m_s` | the anchor of slice $s$: its mean position and mean normal direction |
| $\rho_{is}$, $\xi_{is}$ | $N{\times}M{\times}3$, $N{\times}M{\times}(5+K+P'+Q)$ | `rel`, `geo` | the token-to-anchor separation and the relational invariants formed from it ($P'$ counts the per-token vectors beyond the normal and the global directions, $Q$ the rank-2 inputs; both zero on the aerodynamic tasks) |
| $\pi_{is}$ | $N{\times}M$ | `point_mix` | read-back weights: a softmax over slices $s$ for each token $i$ |
| $\bar\xi_i$, $\gamma_i$ | $N{\times}(5+K)$, $N{\times}d/2$ | `pooled`, `geo_pool` | the invariants pooled over slices, and their projection |
| $Z_s$ | $M{\times}d$ | `z` | the slice state |
| $b_i$ | $N{\times}d$ | `back` | the slice states read back to token $i$ |
| $\hat u_i$ | $N{\times}3$ | `r_hat` | the head's radial direction: from the token's own soft anchor to the token |
| $e_\theta, e_\phi$ | $N{\times}3$ | `spherical_basis` | the tangential complements of $\hat u_i$ against another direction |
| $c_i$, $T_i$ | $N{\times}n_c$, $N{\times}3^r$ per output | `coeffs`, `out[name]` | the head's invariant coefficients and the assembled output fields, one per declared name and rank ($m = 2K + 3$ true basis vectors; a vector costs $m$ coefficients, a symmetric rank-2 tensor $m(m+1)/2 + 1$) |

$\mathrm{LN}$ is LayerNorm over the width; $\mathrm{MLP}$ is Linear–GELU–Linear
with a hidden width of $4d$ (`mlp_ratio`); $W$ with a subscript is a learned
affine map. Definitions use $\equiv$.

## The pass in one picture {#sec-arch-picture}

**From the inputs to the last slice layer, only scalars that are invariant
under rotation, translation and uniform rescaling are computed; vectors are
rebuilt once, at the output.** @fig-isla-pass is the whole surface model.
The three interior arrangements of @sec-arch-modes change which tokens
enter and which the head reads; they add no stage.

```{mermaid}
    LAYER --> HF --> BASIS --> OUT
```

## Stage 1: inputs and the frame {#sec-arch-frame}

**The frame has a length unit and no origin.** The model receives the
sampled boundary, $x_i, n_i, w_i$, and the global inputs $g_k$ and
$\sigma$ (@sec-isla-inputs). It normalizes every direction it is given,
$\hat g_k \equiv g_k / \lvert g_k \rvert$ and $\hat n_i \equiv n_i / \lvert
n_i \rvert$, so a global vector's magnitude never enters (a magnitude that
matters is a global scalar). The one length unit is a normalized two-point
integral of the geometry, with $\tilde w_i \equiv w_i / \sum_j w_j$:

$$
L \equiv \Big( \sum_{i,j} \tilde w_i\, \tilde w_j\, \lvert x_i - x_j \rvert^2 \Big)^{1/2}
      = \Big( 2 \sum_i \tilde w_i\, \lvert x_i - \bar x \rvert^2 \Big)^{1/2},
\qquad
r_i \equiv x_i / L,
\qquad
\ell_i \equiv \log w_i .
$$

The second form is how the code evaluates it (`rms_pairwise_distance`, in
$O(N)$ through the variance identity); the weighted mean $\bar x$ is an
intermediate of this scalar only and is never used as a center. $L$ is
unchanged by a translation or rotation, scales with the geometry, is
unchanged by a uniform rescale of the weights alone because they are
normalized first, and converges under refinement of any boundary whose
normalized measure converges (@sec-isla-frame). The scaled positions $r_i$
are never fed to a learned map; they enter only as differences $r_i - z_s$
in stage 3 and stage 4. The log measure $\ell_i$ is the bias that turns
every routing softmax into a quadrature rule (@sec-isla-quadrature); with
`use_measure_weights=False` (the weights-off ablation) or no weights
supplied it is zero.

## Stage 2: the seed and the embedding {#sec-arch-seed}

**A token's seed is every origin-free scalar the inputs offer, and it is
small.** With no origin, a position alone has no invariant; the only
scalars in $\{\hat n_i, \hat g_k\}$ that survive rotation are the cosines
between them. The seed is therefore

$$
s_i \equiv \big[\, \hat n_i \!\cdot\! \hat g_1,\ \dots,\ \hat n_i \!\cdot\! \hat g_K,\ \beta_i,\ \sigma \,\big]
\quad (K + n_b + S \text{ scalars}),
\qquad
h_i \equiv \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{embed}}(s_i),
$$

where $\beta_i$ are the invariants of the optional per-cell boundary
inputs (`boundary_inputs`: a rank-0 field is its own scalar, a rank-1 field
$v_i$ contributes $v_i \cdot \hat n_i$, $v_i \cdot \hat g_k$ and $\lvert
v_i \rvert$, a rank-2 field its frame contractions, trace and Frobenius
norm; @sec-isla-inputs-rank; $n_b = 0$ on the aerodynamic tasks of this
book) and $\sigma$ the global scalars broadcast to every token. On the surface tasks of this book the seed is a
single number per token, the cosine between the normal and the far-field
direction; if the seed would be empty ($K = n_b = S = 0$) every token starts
from one learned constant. All separation between tokens then comes from
the slice layers, where a token learns where it sits relative to the anchors
(`_seed_invariants`, `embed`).

## Stage 3: the slice layer {#sec-arch-layer}

**A slice layer routes the tokens softly into $M$ slices, forms one anchor
per slice, describes every token relative to every anchor by invariant
scalars, and sends information up to the slices and back down together with
those scalars.** It is the one block that repeats, twelve times, each with
its own parameters (`_SliceBlock`). Its inputs are the token state $h_i$
and the four frame quantities of stage 1, which every layer receives
unchanged: $r_i$, $\hat n_i$, $\hat g_k$, $\ell_i$. Its output is the
updated $h_i$. @fig-isla-layer shows the ten steps; the equations follow in
the same order.

```{mermaid}

%%|   the routing weights to the anchors and the relational invariants, which
%%|   feed back into the routing (the refinement) and forward into the
%%|   read-back. Two softmaxes act on the same logits: over tokens for the
%%|   routing (each slice's weights sum to one, with the measure bias) and over
%%|   slices for the read-back (each token's weights sum to one, without it).
%%|   How to read this: the only tensor that is $N{\times}M$ in the width of

    A0["b. provisional routing a⁰_is = softmax over tokens of λ_is + ℓ_i"]:::fixed
    ANC["c. anchors z_s = Σ_i a⁰_is r_i, m_s = normalize(Σ_i a⁰_is n̂_i) (M×3 each)"]:::fixed
    XI["d. relational invariants ξ_is of (r_i − z_s, n̂_i, m_s, ĝ_k) (N×M×(5+K))"]:::fixed
    REF["e. refinement λ'_is = λ_is + w_g·ξ_is + b_g"]:::learned

    BR["i. h_i += W_b [h_i; b_i; γ_i]"]:::learned

    REF --> PI
    REF --> A1 --> Z --> BACK

    BACK --> BR
    POOL --> BR
    BR --> MLP --> OUT
```

**a. Routing logits.** A learned map of the normalized token state gives a
logit per token–slice pair (`_RoutingLogits`, @sec-isla-routing-forms).
ISLA's form is a temperature $T$ times the cosine between the normalized
state and a learned prototype $p_s$ per slice, which bounds every logit in
$[-T, T]$; the alternative form is an affine map:

$$
\tilde h_i \equiv \mathrm{LN}(h_i), \qquad
\lambda_{is} = T\, \frac{\tilde h_i \cdot p_s}{\lVert \tilde h_i \rVert\, \lVert p_s \rVert} \ \ (\text{cosine},\ T = 10), \qquad
\lambda_{is} = W_a \tilde h_i + b_a \ \ (\text{linear}).
$$

**b. Provisional routing.** A softmax over the *tokens*, for each slice,
with the measure bias:

$$
a^0_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda_{is} + \ell_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\lambda_{js} + \ell_j)} .
$$

Each slice's weights sum to one over the tokens, so anything of the form
$\sum_i a^0_{is} f_i$ is a measure-weighted mean of $f$ over the slice, a
quadrature estimate of a surface integral (`_softmax_over_points`).

**c. Anchors.** From those weights each slice forms its mean position and
its mean normal direction (`z_pos`, `m_s`):

$$
z_s \equiv \sum_i a^0_{is}\, r_i, \qquad
m_s \equiv \frac{\sum_i a^0_{is}\, \hat n_i}{\big\lvert \sum_i a^0_{is}\, \hat n_i \big\rvert} .
$$

Both are weighted sums of vectors that rotate with the body, with weights
that do not, so the anchors rotate and translate with the body
(@sec-isla-slices).

**d. Relational invariants.** For every token–anchor pair, with the
separation $\rho_{is} \equiv r_i - z_s$ and its direction $\hat\rho_{is}$,
the layer forms $5 + K$ scalars (`_relational_invariants`; drawn in
@fig-isla-relational):

$$
\xi_{is} \equiv \big[\,
\lvert\rho_{is}\rvert,\ \log\lvert\rho_{is}\rvert,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat g_1,\ \dots,\ \hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat g_K,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat n_i,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\! m_s,\
\hat n_i\!\cdot\! m_s
\,\big] .
$$

Every entry is a norm or a dot product of vectors that move together, and
every position appears as a difference, so no origin and no axis is
referred to (@sec-isla-relational). A model with rank-1 or rank-2 per-token
inputs appends, in the same place, $\hat\rho_{is} \cdot v$ for every
per-token vector $v$ (the inputs themselves and the vectors $T \hat n_i$,
$T \hat g_k$ derived from a rank-2 input) and $\hat\rho_{is}^{\mathsf T} T
\hat\rho_{is}$ for every rank-2 input, so the width is $5 + K + P' + Q$
(@sec-isla-inputs-rank); on the aerodynamic tasks it is $5 + K$.

**e. Refinement, and the read-back weights.** A linear map of the
invariants to one scalar per pair refines the routing logit, so a slice can
prefer tokens near its anchor, along the global direction from it, or
facing it (`geo_logit`). The *same* refined logits, normalized over the
slices for each token and without the measure bias, are the read-back
weights (`point_mix`):

$$
\lambda'_{is} = \lambda_{is} + w_g \cdot \xi_{is} + b_g, \qquad
\pi_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda'_{is})}{\sum_t \exp(\lambda'_{it})} .
$$

**f. Routing.** The routing weights are recomputed from the refined logits
with the measure bias, exactly as in step b:

$$
a_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda'_{is} + \ell_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\lambda'_{js} + \ell_j)} .
$$

@fig-isla-routing-readback shows the two normalizations side by side on the
airfoil: the same matrix of logits, read one way as "what each slice
averages" and the other way as "where each token reads from".

**g. Slice states.** Each slice aggregates the token states it routes, a
measure-weighted mean, and transforms the result with its own residual MLP
(`slice_mlp`):

$$
Z_s = \sum_i a_{is}\, h_i, \qquad
Z_s \leftarrow Z_s + \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{slice}}(\mathrm{LN}(Z_s)) .
$$

In the surface configuration, this is the only place tokens exchange
information: through $M = 256$ slice states, never pairwise.

**h. Read-back.** Each token reads the slice states with its read-back
weights, and reads the invariants pooled with the same weights, projected
to half the width (`back`, `pooled`, `geo_feat`):

$$
b_i = \sum_s \pi_{is}\, Z_s, \qquad
\bar\xi_i = \sum_s \pi_{is}\, \xi_{is}, \qquad
\gamma_i = W_f\, \bar\xi_i + b_f .
$$

**i. Broadcast.** The token state, what it read, and where it sits are
combined by one affine map into a residual update (`broadcast`):

$$
h_i \leftarrow h_i + W_b\, [\, h_i;\ b_i;\ \gamma_i \,] .
$$

**j. Token MLP.** A pre-norm residual MLP closes the layer (`norm_mlp`,
`mlp`):

$$
h_i \leftarrow h_i + \mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{LN}(h_i)) .
$$

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-routing-readback
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The two softmaxes of a slice layer, on the airfoil with six slices and
#|   eighty cells (the hand-made logits of @fig-isla-slices stand in for the
#|   learned ones; cells are finer near the leading edge). Top: the routing
#|   weights $a_{is}$, a softmax over tokens for each slice with the measure
#|   bias, so each row sums to one and a slice is a quadrature average of the
#|   cells it covers; the fine leading-edge cells receive individually smaller
#|   weights because they stand for less surface. Bottom: the read-back weights
#|   $\pi_{is}$, a softmax over slices for each token without the bias, so each
#|   column sums to one and a token chooses where to read. How to read this:
#|   both matrices come from the same logits; the model has 256 slices and
#|   200,000 tokens per case, so its matrices are much sparser than these.
#| code-fold: true
frac = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(1.0 - 0.6 * np.sin(np.linspace(0, np.pi, 80)) ** 4)]); frac /= frac[-1]
JJ = joukowski(n_cells=80, frac=frac)      # finer cells around the leading edge (mid-arclength)
s_arc = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(JJ["w"])]); s_mid = (s_arc[:-1] + s_arc[1:]) / 2; total = s_arc[-1]
n_sl = 6
centers = (np.arange(n_sl) + 0.5) / n_sl * total
d = np.abs(s_mid[:, None] - centers[None, :]); d = np.minimum(d, total - d)
logits = -(d / (0.06 * total)) ** 2                       # (tokens, slices)
lw_ = np.log(JJ["w"])[:, None]
a = np.exp(logits + lw_); a /= a.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)    # softmax over tokens, per slice
pi = np.exp(logits); pi /= pi.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)        # softmax over slices, per token
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8.0, 4.6), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.35))
for ax, mat, title, vmax in ((axes[0], a.T, r"routing $a_{is}$: softmax over tokens, with the measure bias $\ell_i$; each row sums to 1", None),
                             (axes[1], pi.T, r"read-back $\pi_{is}$: softmax over slices, no bias; each column sums to 1", 1.0)):
    im = ax.imshow(mat, aspect="auto", cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=vmax if vmax else mat.max(), interpolation="nearest")
    ax.grid(False); ax.set_yticks(range(n_sl)); ax.set_yticklabels([f"slice {k + 1}" for k in range(n_sl)], fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9.5, loc="left", color=INK)
    for sp in ax.spines.values(): sp.set_visible(False)
    cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.03, pad=0.01); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=8); cb.outline.set_visible(False)
    cb.set_label("weight [–]", fontsize=8.5)
i_le = int(np.argmin(JJ["mid"][:, 0]))
axes[1].set_xlabel("token $i$ along the surface, from the trailing edge around the leading edge and back [index]", fontsize=9)
for ax in axes:
    ax.axvline(i_le, color=WHITE, lw=1.0, ls="--")
axes[1].text(i_le + 0.8, n_sl - 0.55, "leading edge", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=WHITE)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Two identities the implementation relies on"}
**Pool first, then project.** The invariants $\xi_{is}$ are $N{\times}M{\times}(5+K)$.
Projecting each pair to width $d/2$ and then pooling would make autograd
store an $N{\times}M{\times}d/2$ tensor per layer; because the projection is
affine and $\pi_{is}$ sums to one over slices,
$\sum_s \pi_{is}(W_f \xi_{is} + b_f) = W_f \sum_s \pi_{is} \xi_{is} + b_f$,
so the code pools first and saves only $N{\times}(5+K)$. The identity is
tested at $10^{-12}$ (@sec-isla-contracts).

**Rebuild the geometry in the backward pass.** Steps c to e and the pooling
of step h are one *geometry region* per layer (`_geo_region`): a function
of $(\lambda, r, \hat n, \hat g, z, m)$ with no parameters but $w_g, b_g$.
On the eager path, `geo_checkpoint=True` recomputes its $N{\times}M{\times}\cdot$
intermediates in the backward pass instead of storing them, with
bitwise-identical outputs and gradients; the fused Triton kernel
(`geo_kernel="fused"`, the automatic choice on CUDA with one global vector
and at most 1,024 slices) evaluates the same region without ever
materializing them, with the recompute built in (@sec-using-cost).
:::

## Stage 4: the head frame {#sec-arch-head-frame}

**The vector head needs one direction per token that points from the body
to the token, and ISLA takes it from the token's own soft anchor, not from
a center.** After the last layer, one more routing map (`frame_assign`,
acting on the final $h_i$) gives logits $\lambda^f_{is}$. Read one way they
give anchors, read the other way they give each token's soft assignment:

$$
a^f_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda^f_{is} + \ell_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\lambda^f_{js} + \ell_j)}, \qquad
z^f_s = \sum_i a^f_{is}\, r_i, \qquad
\beta_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda^f_{is})}{\sum_t \exp(\lambda^f_{it})}, \qquad
u_i = r_i - \sum_s \beta_{is}\, z^f_s, \qquad
\hat u_i = u_i / \lvert u_i \rvert .
$$

$u_i$ is a difference of positions, so $\hat u_i$ rotates with the body and
is unchanged by a translation; no centroid appears (`a_f`, `z_f`, `b_f`,
`r_hat`; the construction is @fig-isla-basis).

## Stage 5: the head {#sec-arch-head}

**One linear head produces every output's invariant coefficients, and each
output of declared rank $r$ is contracted from them over tensor products of
$r$ vectors the token already has.** On the normalized final state
(`norm_out`, `head`):

$$
c_i = W_h\, \mathrm{LN}(h_i) + b_h, \qquad c_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n_c},
$$

with $n_c$ the sum over the declared outputs of their coefficient counts.
The true basis at token $i$, in the order the code stacks it, is

$$
t_i = \big\{\, \hat g_1, \dots, \hat g_K,\ \hat n_i,\ \hat u_i,\
e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat n_i),\ e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat g_1),\ \dots \,\big\}
\quad (m = 2K + 3 \text{ vectors}),
$$

with the tangential complement of $\hat u$ against a second direction
$\hat a$ defined, unnormalized, as

$$
e_\theta(\hat u, \hat a) \equiv -\hat a + (\hat a \cdot \hat u)\, \hat u
$$

(`spherical_basis` with `normalize_basis_vectors=False`; it vanishes
smoothly where $\hat u \parallel \hat a$, which is why it is left
unnormalized), and the pseudovector basis is the set of cross products of
the primaries $\{\hat g_k, \hat n_i, \hat u_i\}$ ($p = \binom{K+2}{2}$
vectors). An output declared with rank $r$ and even parity is

$$
T_i = \sum_{j_1 \dots j_r} c_{i\, j_1 \dots j_r}\; t_{i j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes t_{i j_r}
\;+\; \sum_k c_{ik}^{\mathrm{iso}}\, I_k ,
$$

where the isotropic tensors $I_k$ are the identity at rank 2 and the three
products of Kronecker deltas at rank 4 (their symmetric sum for a symmetric
spec); a symmetric spec carries one coefficient per unordered multi-index,
and an odd-parity spec replaces exactly one factor by a pseudovector (with
the Levi-Civita symbol as the isotropic term at rank 3). The code gathers
the free coefficients into the full coefficient tensor over ordered
multi-indices and contracts one index at a time, so the basis of $m^r$
products is never materialized (`_OutputLayout`, `_assemble_output`). The
coefficient counts per output are $1$ at rank 0, $m$ at rank 1 ($5$ with
one global direction), $m^2 + 1$ or $m(m+1)/2 + 1$ (symmetric) at rank 2
($26$ or $16$), $m^3$ or $\binom{m+2}{3}$ at rank 3, $m^4 + 3$ or
$\binom{m+3}{4} + 1$ at rank 4; the class refuses ranks above 4. The model
returns a dictionary keyed by the output names (pressure, a rank-0 field of
shape $N$; wall shear stress, a rank-1 field of shape $N{\times}3$, in every
surface result of the book). Under an orthogonal map $R$ every true basis
vector maps as $R t$, every pseudovector as $\det(R)\, R t$, and every
coefficient is unchanged, so an even output maps as $R^{\otimes r} T$ and an
odd one as $\det(R)\, R^{\otimes r} T$: that is the covariance proof, for
rotations and reflections alike, and @sec-isla-contracts lists the tests
that check it.

## Where the parameters are {#sec-arch-params}

**Almost all of ISLA's parameters are ordinary MLPs; the geometry costs
seven numbers per layer.** @tbl-isla-params counts them from the class at
two widths, 12 layers and 256 slices.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-isla-params
#| output: asis
import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import torch
from physicsnemo.experimental.models import ISLA
cnt = lambda mod: sum(p.numel() for p in mod.parameters())
widths = (192, 384)
models = {w: ISLA(outputs={"pressure": 0, "wss": 1}, global_inputs={"freestream": 1}, hidden=w, n_layers=12, n_slices=256) for w in widths}
def rows_for(m):
    blk = m.blocks[0]
    return [
        ("embedding MLP (stage 2)", "`embed`", cnt(m.embed), 1),
        ("routing map, with its LayerNorm (step a)", "`norm_assign`, `assign`", cnt(blk.norm_assign) + cnt(blk.assign), 12),
        ("routing refinement (step e)", "`geo_logit`", cnt(blk.geo_logit), 12),
        ("pooled-invariant projection (step h)", "`geo_feat`", cnt(blk.geo_feat), 12),
        ("slice MLP, with its LayerNorm (step g)", "`slice_mlp`", cnt(blk.slice_mlp), 12),
        ("broadcast (step i)", "`broadcast`", cnt(blk.broadcast), 12),
        ("token MLP, with its LayerNorm (step j)", "`norm_mlp`, `mlp`", cnt(blk.norm_mlp) + cnt(blk.mlp), 12),
        ("head-frame routing map (stage 4)", "`frame_assign`", cnt(m.frame_assign), 1),
        ("head, with its LayerNorm (stage 5)", "`norm_out`, `head`", cnt(m.norm_out) + cnt(m.head), 1),
    ]
R = {w: rows_for(models[w]) for w in widths}
totals = {w: cnt(models[w]) for w in widths}
for w in widths:
    assert sum(c * n for _, _, c, n in R[w]) == totals[w]
out = "| component | code | copies | parameters in all, 192 wide | share | parameters in all, 384 wide | share |\n|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|\n"
for (name, code, c192, n), (_, _, c384, _) in zip(R[192], R[384]):
    out += (f"| {name} | {code} | {n} | {c192 * n:,} | {100 * c192 * n / totals[192]:.1f}% "
            f"| {c384 * n:,} | {100 * c384 * n / totals[384]:.1f}% |\n")
out += f"| **total** | | | **{totals[192]:,}** | 100% | **{totals[384]:,}** | 100% |\n"
out += ("\n: Parameter count of ISLA at 12 layers, 256 slices, one scalar and one vector output and one global vector input, at widths 192 and 384, "
        "computed from the class as the page renders. How to read this: the shares barely move with width because every large component is "
        "quadratic in it; the routing maps and the geometry are the exceptions. {#tbl-isla-params}\n")
print(out)
```

The two per-layer MLPs hold four fifths of the total; the broadcast maps
and the routing maps (at $d \times M$ each) hold most of the rest. Width $d$
therefore sets the count quadratically and the slice count $M$ linearly,
which is why the capacity ladders of @sec-equal-budget move width and not
slices.

## The interior arrangements {#sec-arch-modes}

**Two arrangements of tokens and queries share the five stages; they
differ in which points are tokens and which the head reads.**
@fig-isla-modes places them side by side. Everything above described the
first; every interior result of the book uses the second. A third, the
optional passive decoder, is exactly query-independent at a measured
accuracy price and is described in @sec-arch-passive-decoder.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-isla-modes
%%| fig-cap: >
%%|   The two arrangements of ISLA. Surface: the boundary cells are the
%%|   tokens and the head reads every one of them. Interior with query tokens:
%%|   interior points join the encoder as interacting tokens with a learned
%%|   routing mass, and the head reads them alone (the configuration the
%%|   interior results of the book use). How to read this: the slice layer,
%%|   head frame and head are the same modules in both; only the token set
%%|   and which tokens the head reads change. The optional passive decoder
%%|   (@sec-arch-passive-decoder) is not drawn.
flowchart LR
    classDef data fill:#f4f3ee,stroke:#898781,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef learned fill:#e6f0fb,stroke:#2a78d6,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef fixed fill:#ffffff,stroke:#2a78d6,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef aqua fill:#e3f6ef,stroke:#1baf7a,color:#0b0b0b

    subgraph S["surface (the default)"]
        direction TB
        S1["boundary tokens (N)"]:::data
        S2["slice layers × 12"]:::learned
        S3["head frame + head on all N tokens"]:::learned
        S1 --> S2 --> S3
    end
    subgraph Q["interior, queries as tokens (query_tokens)"]
        direction TB
        Q1["boundary tokens (N)"]:::data
        Q2["query tokens (Q): position, SDF gradient as normal,<br/>signed distance as scalar; learned routing mass"]:::aqua
        Q3["slice layers × 12 on all N + Q tokens"]:::learned
        Q4["head frame + head on the Q query tokens"]:::learned
        Q1 --> Q3
        Q2 --> Q3 --> Q4
    end
```

**Queries as tokens** (`query_tokens=True`; @sec-interior-query-tokens).
Each interior point $q$ arrives with a normal (the gradient of the signed
distance field) and, in this book, one per-query scalar, the signed
distance $\delta_q$ to the wall. It is placed in the same frame, seeded like
a boundary cell with zeros in the boundary-scalar channel, and given a
learned type offset and a scalar embedding:

$$
r_q = x_q / L, \qquad
h_q = \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{embed}}(s_q) + t_{\mathrm{q}}
      + \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{qs}}\!\big(\,[\, \delta_q / L,\ \operatorname{sign}(\delta_q) \log(\lvert \delta_q \rvert / L + \epsilon) \,]\big) .
$$

Its measure bias is not an area but a learned share of the boundary's total
measure, split equally over the $Q$ queries (`query_mass="source_total"`):

$$
\ell_q = \omega + \log \sum_{i \le N} w_i - \log Q ,
$$

so re-representing the same surface on finer cells changes nothing, and
rescaling the geometry shifts every token's bias by the same amount. The
$N + Q$ tokens then run through the twelve slice layers together; the head
frame builds its anchors from all of them, and the head reads the $Q$ query
tokens only. The arrangement is exactly covariant and not query-independent
(@sec-isla-contracts).

### The optional passive decoder {#sec-arch-passive-decoder}

**A prediction from the interacting arrangement depends on which other
points are in the request. The class keeps a switch that removes that
dependence exactly, and no interior result in this book uses it, because
its accuracy price is several-fold on every field.** The note below is
the one place the book describes it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The passive decoder: exact query independence, and why the interior results do not use it"}

**What it is.** With `query_independent=True` the encoder runs on the
boundary alone; the queries never enter it. One more routing map on the
final state (`final_assign`) summarizes the encoder once into slice states
$Z_s$ and anchors $z_s, m_s$ exactly as steps b, c and g do. Each query,
seeded and embedded as a query token would be (with its own scalar
embedding), then passes through `n_decoder_layers` (four by default)
**read blocks** (`_ReadBlock`), each of which forms the relational
invariants $\xi_{qs}$ against the final anchors, reads over the slices, and
reads the encoder states near the query through a measure-weighted
Gaussian kernel of width $\varrho$ (`local_readout_rho`, 0.02 length units):

$$
\pi_{qs} = \mathrm{softmax}_s\big(\lambda_{qs} + w_g \!\cdot\! \xi_{qs} + b_g\big), \qquad
h_q \leftarrow h_q + W_b\, \big[\, h_q;\ \textstyle\sum_s \pi_{qs} Z_s;\ W_f \sum_s \pi_{qs}\, \xi_{qs} + b_f \,\big],
$$

$$
\kappa_{qi} = \frac{\exp(-\lvert r_q - r_i \rvert^2 / \varrho^2 + \ell_i)}{\sum_j \exp(-\lvert r_q - r_j \rvert^2 / \varrho^2 + \ell_j)}, \qquad
h_q \leftarrow h_q + W_l\, \big[\, h_q;\ \textstyle\sum_i \kappa_{qi}\, h_i \,\big], \qquad
h_q \leftarrow h_q + \mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{LN}(h_q)) .
$$

Nothing in a read block writes into the encoder, so the prediction at a
query is a function of the boundary and that query alone. The head frame's
anchors come from the encoder tokens and its soft assignment $\beta_{qs}$
from the query state; the head is stage 5 unchanged. The property is a
contract of the code, not of a checkpoint: `test_query_set_independence`
checks in float64 that 50 queries predicted alone equal the same 50 among
150 to $10^{-12}$ with zero relative tolerance (@sec-isla-contracts), and
on a trained checkpoint the same sentinel points predicted alone, with
2,000 companions and with 40,000 move by exactly 0.000 in float32
(@sec-nb-qmass-verdict). With `support_tokens=True` a per-case set of
interior *support* points joins the encoder as interacting tokens (seeded
and weighted like query tokens) while the requested queries are still
decoded read-only, which keeps the contract with more of the interior in
view. Every contract of @sec-isla-contracts holds in this mode; the
read-only path with boundary scalars fails on a shape when source and
query counts differ, and no number in the book uses that pair.

**Why the interior results use interacting query tokens instead.** The
price was measured on the DrivAerML Volume task in float32 on the 48
validation cars with two seeds, at the 10,000-cell exploration budget
(the reporting protocol of @sec-protocol is 200,000 cells; these numbers
are a labeled mechanism measurement, not an accuracy claim, and the
100,000-cell re-measurement is pending under PROTOCOL-REDO,
@sec-nb-protocol-redo-prereg). Against the interacting query tokens with
the signed distance (0.0547 / 0.0796 / 0.1116 on pressure / velocity /
eddy viscosity):

| passive arm (10,000 boundary cells and queries, float32) | pressure | velocity | eddy viscosity | passive ÷ interacting |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|
| twelve read blocks, same inputs as the query tokens (matched depth and inputs) | 0.0890 | 0.1201 | 0.2305 | 1.63 / 1.51 / 2.07 |
| twelve read blocks over an interacting interior support set carrying the signed distance | 0.0781 | 0.1068 | 0.2689 | 1.43 / 1.34 / 2.41 |
| the complete passive configuration as built: four read blocks, signed-distance gradient as the query normal, no signed-distance scalar | 0.1572 | 0.3052 | 0.3736 | 2.87 / 3.83 / 3.35 |

: The passive decoder's price against the interacting query tokens on the
DrivAerML Volume task (relative L2, arithmetic mean over 48 validation
cars and two seeds, float32, 10,000 boundary cells and 10,000 queries per
car, 500 epochs). Ratios are passive ÷ interacting, above one against the
passive decoder; seed spreads are at most 2% for the passive arms and 9%
for the interacting one, so every ratio is resolved. The complete
configuration is 3.06 / 2.81 / 4.25 times GeoTransolver-volume's error on
the same points. Data:
research/transfer_program/studies/computational_support/d1_verdict_2026-09-10.json
(first two rows); @sec-nb-fp32-interior-family and
@sec-nb-fp32-reeval-verdict-interior (third row). {#tbl-arch-passive-price}

The two matched rows locate the price: it is not depth (twelve read
blocks against four, both over the support set, change pressure by 13%)
and not interior context (the interacting support set with the signed
distance changes it by 12% and makes eddy viscosity worse), but the
computation the interacting queries receive at the requested points
through every slice layer. That is why admitting the queries as tokens
closes most of the gap to GeoTransolver-volume on pressure with no extra
parameters (@sec-interior-results), and why the passive route is closed
for ISLA at matched depth and inputs. The verdict rests on one dataset:
the passive decoder has not been trained on AirfRANS.

**What the interacting tokens give up.** A prediction at a point is a
function of the whole request. The size of the dependence is measured at
the same exploration budget (@sec-interior-companion, QCOUNT,
@sec-nb-qcount-verdict): the reference checkpoint trained at 10,000
requests and scored at 2,000 loses 1.38x / 1.59x / 1.49x on pressure /
velocity / eddy viscosity, and at 40,000 it moves by 3% and improves;
training over request sizes 2,000 to 20,000 reduces the 2,000-request
penalty to 1.24x / 1.31x / 1.31x at a 3.7% pressure cost and does not
remove it. The default query mass `query_mass="source_total"` removes the
count scaling of the routing weight by construction; the dependence
through the shared slices remains. The working rule is to deploy the
interacting configuration at its training request count and to state
that count with every interior number.

**Practical considerations.** The passive decoder is the right tool when
the deployment needs the contract rather than the last factor of
accuracy:

- *Encode once, decode many.* The encoder's final slice states and
  anchors are a fixed summary of one boundary; any number of query
  batches can be decoded from it later, in any chunking, and the answer
  at a point never changes. The interacting arrangement recomputes the
  slice layers for every request and its answer depends on the batch.
- *Streaming or chunked inference over arbitrary point sets.* A
  streamline traced point by point, a probe plane added after the fact, a
  domain too large for one forward pass: with the passive decoder the
  chunks are exactly consistent with each other and with the whole; with
  the interacting decoder each chunk must be filled to the training count
  and adjacent chunks disagree at shared points by the companion
  sensitivity above.
- *Reproducibility and certification.* A per-point prediction that is a
  pure function of the boundary and the point is auditable and identical
  across requests; the interacting prediction is identical only for an
  identical request.
- *Memory.* The passive decoder's cost in queries is linear and separable
  from the encoder: queries do not attend to one another. The interacting
  arrangement's token set is $N + Q$: at the reporting protocol, 200,000
  boundary cells and 200,000 queries are a 400,000-token case, whose
  training peak on the cost grid is 53.5 GB for ISLA-192 against 27 GB for
  200,000 tokens (@sec-cost-sweep), with the fused geometry kernel; on
  the eager fallback the geometry region is rebuilt in the
  backward pass (`geo_checkpoint`) to hold memory. The passive decoder is
  not free of its own footprint: its local readout saves a $4{,}096 \times
  Q$ kernel per chunk for the backward pass, so 200,000 queries against
  200,000 boundary tokens exceed one GB300 in training (about 500 GB of
  saved kernels), and the pending re-measurement runs at 100,000;
  recomputing those chunks in backward is the queued engineering fix
  (@sec-nb-protocol-redo-prereg).

The interacting arrangement is the default whenever the evaluation point
set is fixed and available in full, in batch inference, and wherever
accuracy is the objective, which is every interior result of this book.
The passive decoder stays supported as a switch at the price in
@tbl-arch-passive-price; nothing in the program has found a way to keep
its contract at the interacting configuration's accuracy, and the two
attempts (latent volume tokens, an interacting support set) are recorded
in @sec-interior-negatives and in the table above.

:::

## What the trained routing looks like {#sec-arch-routing-trained}

**On a trained model a slice is a region of the body. A token's dominant
slice is a patch of surface with an anchor inside the body, the first
layer routes nearly everything into a handful of slices, and the deep
layers spread the mass over most of the 256 while each token stays soft.**
Every routing picture in Part I so far drew hand-made routing weights on the
airfoil; this section reads the real ones out of trained checkpoints, so
the reader can see what @sec-isla-slices promised. The instrument is a
wrapper around the routing softmax over tokens (`_softmax_over_points`,
step f) with pre- and post-hooks on each `_SliceBlock` delimiting the two
calls a block makes (step b's provisional pass and step f's refined pass);
the block's second call is read. From the recorded refined logits the
read-back weights $\pi_{is}$ of step e, a softmax over the slices without
the measure bias, are each token's **soft assignment**; the **dominant
slice** of a token is $\arg\max_s \pi_{is}$, the **mass** of a slice is
$q_s \equiv \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \pi_{is}$ (the slices' share of the tokens,
summing to one), and the **effective number of slices** is
$M_{\mathrm{eff}} \equiv \exp(-\sum_s q_s \log q_s)$, which is 256 when
every slice carries the same mass and 1 when one slice carries all of it.
The anchors are step c's $z_s$, drawn in the dataset's coordinates. Each
checkpoint is the final one of a completed reference-configuration run
(384 wide, 12 layers, 256 slices, cosine routing), run in float32 on the
first case of its validation loader with the geometry kernel it trained
with; the numbers in this section are computed from the stored weights as
the page renders.

```{python}
#| label: setup-routing-trained
#| include: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
SL = RES / "probes" / "slices_2026-09-22"
PF = RES / "problem_figures_2026-09-22"
M_SL = 256

def load_slices(run):
    z = np.load(SL / f"{run}_case0.npz"); meta = json.load(open(SL / f"{run}_case0.json"))
    return {k: z[k] for k in z.files}, meta

def n_eff(q):
    return float(np.exp(-(q * np.log(q + 1e-30)).sum()))

SLICE_COLS = slice_colors(M_SL)

def partition_colors(dom, conf, floor=0.25):
    """Dominant-slice color, faded toward paper where the token is undecided (its largest pi_is is small)."""
    c = SLICE_COLS[dom].copy(); a = np.clip(conf / max(np.quantile(conf, 0.95), 1e-6), floor, 1.0)
    paper = np.array([0.96, 0.96, 0.95, 1.0])
    return a[:, None] * c + (1 - a[:, None]) * paper

def draw_anchors(ax, d, li, scale=1.0, dims=(0, 1), s=50):
    q = d["q"][li]; active = np.flatnonzero(q > 1.0 / M_SL); A = d["anchors"][li][active] * scale
    ax.scatter(A[:, dims[0]], A[:, dims[1]], marker="*", s=s, c=SLICE_COLS[active], edgecolors=INK, linewidths=0.45, zorder=5)
    return len(active)

DR, DRm = load_slices("ref_isla_r1_dr435_seed42")
T2, T2m = load_slices("so_t2d_isla_r1_frame_n64_seed42")
AF, AFm = load_slices("ref_isla_r1_af_seed42")
LG, LGm = load_slices("so_lug_isla_r1_n300_seed43")
L_REF_DR = json.load(open(PF / "drivaer.json"))["L_ref"]        # the recipe divides DrivAerML positions by L_ref = 5 m
RUNS = {"DrivAerML Surface task, 435 cars": (DR, DRm), "AirfRANS interior task, 800 airfoils": (AF, AFm),
        "PLAID Tensile2d with the frame, 64 cases": (T2, T2m), "GINOT lug, 300 cases": (LG, LGm)}
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-routing-partition-drivaer
#| fig-cap: >
#|   How the trained ISLA partitions a car, DrivAerML Surface task. Side
#|   view of the 200,000 boundary tokens of one validation car (a 60,000-token
#|   subset drawn), each colored by its dominant slice at the first, sixth and
#|   last slice layer; a token whose largest soft assignment is small is faded
#|   toward the paper. Stars are the anchors $z_s$ of the slices whose mass
#|   exceeds the uniform share $1/M$, in the slice's color. How to read this:
#|   slice colors are labels and repeat (twenty hues for 256 slices), so two
#|   distant patches of one hue are usually different slices; what the picture
#|   shows is the granularity and placement of the partition, not the identity
#|   of any slice. The tokens carry no coordinates; the patches follow from the
#|   token states and the relational invariants alone. Data:
#|   results/probes/slices_2026-09-22/ref_isla_r1_dr435_seed42_case0.npz
#|   (epoch 500, float32, the run's fused kernel).
#| code-fold: true
P = DR["points"][DR["keep"]] * L_REF_DR
layers = [int(i) for i in DR["top_layers"]]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(8, 7.0), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.25))
for ax, li in zip(axes, layers):
    depth_scatter(ax, P[:, [0, 2]], P[:, 1], partition_colors(DR["dominant"][li].astype(int), DR["pi_max"][li].astype(float)), s=2.0)
    map_axes(ax)
    n_act = draw_anchors(ax, DR, li, scale=L_REF_DR, dims=(0, 2))
    ax.set_title(f"layer {li + 1} of 12: effective number of slices {n_eff(DR['q'][li]):.0f}; {n_act} slices above the uniform mass (stars: their anchors)", fontsize=9.5)
    ax.set_ylabel("z [m]")
axes[-1].set_xlabel("x [m]  (far-field flow along $+x$)")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-routing-weights-drivaer
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Three individual slices of the sixth layer on the same car: the soft
#|   assignment $\pi_{is}$ of every token to the slice, as heat, for the three
#|   slices that are the dominant slice of the most tokens, each seen from the
#|   side (left) and from below (right). The star is the slice's anchor. How to
#|   read this: a slice is a soft region, brightest at its core and fading
#|   over its neighbors; the anchor is the routing-weighted mean position of
#|   the region and sits inside the body when the region wraps around it. The
#|   largest territories of this layer are on the wheels and the underbody,
#|   where the surface mesh is finest and the sampled tokens densest, which is
#|   why the view from below is drawn. Each panel's color scale runs to the
#|   slice's own 99.9th percentile of $\pi_{is}$; the printed $q_s$ is the
#|   slice's mass, its share of all tokens. Data:
#|   results/probes/slices_2026-09-22/ref_isla_r1_dr435_seed42_case0.npz.
#| code-fold: true
li_pos = 1; L6 = int(DR["top_layers"][li_pos]); ts = DR["top_slices"][li_pos][:3]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(8, 5.8), gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.6, wspace=0.08, width_ratios=[1, 1]))
for j, (ax_side, ax_below) in enumerate(axes):
    pi = DR["top_pi"][li_pos][:, j].astype(float); vmax = max(0.2, float(np.quantile(pi, 0.999)))
    sc = depth_scatter(ax_side, P[:, [0, 2]], P[:, 1], pi, s=1.6, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=vmax)
    depth_scatter(ax_below, P[:, [0, 1]], -P[:, 2], pi, s=1.6, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=vmax)
    a = DR["anchors"][L6][ts[j]] * L_REF_DR
    ax_side.plot(a[0], a[2], marker="*", ms=12, color=WHITE, mec=INK, mew=0.8, zorder=5)
    ax_below.plot(a[0], a[1], marker="*", ms=12, color=WHITE, mec=INK, mew=0.8, zorder=5)
    for ax in (ax_side, ax_below):
        map_axes(ax)
    n_dom = int((DR["dominant"][L6] == ts[j]).sum())
    ax_side.set_title(f"slice {int(ts[j])}: $q_s$ = {DR['q'][L6][ts[j]]:.3f}, dominant for {n_dom:,} of {len(P):,} tokens; side view", fontsize=8.2)
    ax_below.set_title("the same slice from below", fontsize=8.2, loc="right")
    ax_side.set_ylabel("z [m]"); ax_below.set_ylabel("y [m]"); ax_below.yaxis.set_label_position("right"); ax_below.yaxis.tick_right()
    cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=[ax_side, ax_below], fraction=0.015, pad=0.08); cb.outline.set_visible(False); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
    cb.set_label(r"$\pi_{is}$ [–]", fontsize=8)
for ax in axes[-1]:
    ax.set_xlabel("x [m]")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: routing-trained-numbers

def undecided(d, li, thr=0.5):
    return 100.0 * float((d["pi_max"][li].astype(float) < thr).mean())
ne_dr = [n_eff(DR["q"][li]) for li in range(12)]; ne_t2 = [n_eff(T2["q"][li]) for li in range(12)]
dr_l1_top = np.sort(DR["q"][0])[::-1]
print(
    f"**What the pictures show.** In the first layer the car model routes with an effective number of {ne_dr[0]:.0f} slices "
    f"and its heaviest slice holds {100 * dr_l1_top[0]:.0f}% of the soft mass: that layer's routing map sees only the embedded seed "
    f"(each normal against the far-field direction), refined by the geometry against anchors formed from that same seed, and a car's "
    f"surface offers few distinct values of it. From the "
    f"second layer on the token states carry position through the relational invariants and the effective number rises to "
    f"{min(ne_dr[1:6]):.0f} to {max(ne_dr[1:6]):.0f} in layers 2 to 6 and {min(ne_dr[6:]):.0f} to {max(ne_dr[6:]):.0f} in layers 7 to 12. "
    f"The specimen model, whose seed already carries the boundary labels, the frame and six global scalars, starts at {ne_t2[0]:.0f} "
    f"and stays between {min(ne_t2):.0f} and {max(ne_t2):.0f}. The assignment is soft throughout: in the sixth layer "
    f"{undecided(DR, 5):.0f}% of the car's tokens and {undecided(T2, 5):.0f}% of the specimen's give no single slice more than half "
    f"their weight, and in the last layer {undecided(DR, 11):.0f}% and {undecided(T2, 11):.0f}%. Anchors sit inside the body, not on "
    f"it, as the weighted mean of a patch that wraps a wheel or a neck must. These are descriptions of one validation case of one "
    f"seed per model; they show the granularity of the learned partition and are not a claim about accuracy."
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How the weights were read, and what the earlier routing probes measured"}
The wrapper records the input and output of every call of
`_softmax_over_points`; a slice block calls it twice, once with the
provisional logits (step b, used only to place the anchors) and once with
the refined logits (step f). Forward pre-hooks on the blocks record where
each block's calls start and end, and the block's last call is read; its
input is $\lambda'_{is} + \ell_i$, so subtracting the measure bias $\ell_i$
(taken from the block's second argument) and normalizing over slices gives
$\pi_{is}$ exactly as step e computes it. The earlier routing probes
(@sec-nb-routingsat-erratum) indexed the flat list of calls, so their
"layer $i$" was block $\lfloor i/2 \rfloor$, pass $i \bmod 2$; the per-layer
numbers here are per block. The recorded arrays are stored subsampled to
60,000 tokens per case for the pictures; the masses and effective numbers
are computed over every token before subsampling. Probe:
`results/probes/slices_2026-09-22/slices_probe.py`.
:::

## What the pass never does {#sec-arch-never}

**The contracts of @sec-isla-contracts are absences, and two of them can be
read off the stages directly.**

- **No coordinate reaches a learned map, and no center is estimated.**
  $r_i$ enters only as $r_i - z_s$ (step d), $r_i - \sum_s \beta_{is} z^f_s$
  (stage 4) and $\lvert r_q - r_i \rvert$ (the local readout); every learned
  input is a norm, a dot product, a log of one of those, or a supplied
  scalar. The one mean position computed, inside $L$, is consumed by a
  scalar; anchors are means over *slices*, not over the body, and only
  their differences from tokens are used.
- **No positional encoding, no pairwise attention.** Tokens communicate
  only through the $M$ slice states, and the routing that decides which
  slice a token joins is a function of the token's state and its relation
  to the anchors.

## The switches {#sec-arch-switches}

**The class has one frame and a small set of switches; each names the stage
it changes.** The recipe's surface and interior configurations are in
@sec-using-config.

| flag (default) | stage | what it changes |
|---|---|---|
| `hidden` (256 in the class; the recipe's width is in @sec-using-config), `n_layers` (12), `n_slices` (256), `mlp_ratio` (4) | all | $d$, the number of slice layers, $M$, and the MLP expansion |
| `outputs` (required) | 5 | the output fields by name and rank spec (`{pressure: 0, wss: 1, stress: {rank: 2, symmetric: true}}`; `parity: odd` for a pseudotensor); each field costs the coefficient count of @sec-arch-head and is returned under its name |
| `global_inputs` (none) | 1, 2, 3d, 5 | the per-case fields by name and rank: each rank-1 field is a global direction $\hat g_k$ (one seed cosine, one relational cosine, two basis vectors); each rank-0 field (with `channels` for a parameter vector) widens the seed |
| `boundary_inputs` (none) | 2, 3d | per-cell fields by name and rank 0 to 2: their invariants $\beta_i$ join the seed (non-boundary tokens carry zeros), and rank-1 and rank-2 fields add their contractions with $\hat\rho_{is}$ to the relational invariants (@sec-isla-inputs-rank) |
| `query_inputs` (none), `query_scalar_scale` (`"length"`) | modes | per-query fields by name and rank 0 to 2, carried by the query, support and passive-query tokens through their own embedding; rank-0 fields are divided by $L$ and paired with a signed log under `"length"` |
| `scale_mode` (`"rms_distance"`) | 1 | the length unit: the measure-weighted RMS pairwise distance of the sample |
| `use_measure_weights` (on) | 3b, 3f, 4 | the measure bias $\ell_i$; off is the weights-off ablation |
| `routing_norm` (`"cosine"`), `routing_temperature` (10) | 3a, 4 | the form of every routing map: the bounded cosine against learned prototypes, or `"linear"`, the affine alternative (@sec-isla-routing-forms) |
| `use_relational_geo` (on) | 3d, 3e, 3h | the relational invariants in the refinement and the read-back; off is the feature-only slicing ablation |
| `query_tokens` (off), `query_mass` (`"source_total"`) | modes | the interacting interior arrangement and the queries' routing mass: a learned share of the total boundary measure, or `"geometric_mean"`, a learned factor times the geometric mean of the source weights (which depends on the boundary refinement) |
| `query_independent` (off), `n_decoder_layers` (4), `local_readout_rho` (0.02), `support_tokens` (off) | modes | the optional passive decoder (exactly query-independent, at the accuracy price in @sec-arch-passive-decoder), its depth, its local-readout width, and its optional interacting support set |
| `geo_kernel` (`None`, automatic), `geo_checkpoint` (off), `fast_point_softmax` (on) | 3c–3e, 3h | how the geometry region is executed: `None` resolves at the first forward pass to `"fused"` (the Triton kernel) when the inputs are on CUDA, Triton is importable, there is one global direction, at most 1,024 slices and no rank-1 or rank-2 per-token input, and to `"eager"` (the PyTorch region) otherwise; either name forces that path, and `"fused"` raises where its constraints fail. `geo_checkpoint` rebuilds the eager region in backward instead of storing it; `fast_point_softmax` selects the row-parallel softmax kernel. None changes the function computed beyond roundoff |
| `eps` ($10^{-12}$) | 1, 3c, 3d, 4 | the floor under every norm and logarithm |
